youtube.baslik: Case: Fluctuating Low-Frequency Loss in Meniere's | Lesson 275 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
In a fictional adult case, we work step by step through the audiological findings of Meniere's disease: low-frequency sensorineural loss, the audiometric criterion of the Barany Society, comparing serial audiograms, the SP/AP ratio in ECochG, the caloric and vHIT dissociation, VEMP, and the audiologist's role in counseling and reporting.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Lopez-Escamez et al., Diagnostic criteria for Meniere's disease (Journal of Vestibular Research, 2015); Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology; Hall, New Handbook of Auditory Evoked Responses; Jacobson and Shepard, Balance Function Assessment and Management.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we work through an adult case with recurrent vertigo attacks and a fluctuating hearing loss in the right ear.
We will compare serial audiograms, look at electrophysiological and vestibular test findings, and see the audiologist's role.

maddeler.metin: Each attack one to three hours

cumleler: Our case is fictional: a forty-five-year-old person referred by an ENT physician for recurrent attacks of dizziness.
In the last six months there were three spontaneous spinning attacks, with nausea and vomiting.
Each attack lasted one to three hours; between attacks the person feels largely well.
Before attacks, fullness and a low-pitched, roaring tinnitus increase in the right ear.
The person says hearing in the right ear drops during and after an attack, then partly recovers.
There is no headache, light sensitivity or neurological symptom; these details are recorded for the differential diagnosis.

notlar.metin: Hydrops is _not the same_ as Meniere's

cumleler: The structural change thought to lie behind these symptoms is endolymphatic hydrops.
In hydrops, endolymph in the middle scala, the scala media, increases and Reissner's membrane bulges toward the scala vestibuli.
Hydrops usually affects the region near the cochlear apex first, that is, the low-frequency region.
This explains why the loss in Meniere's disease often begins in the low frequencies.
But hydrops can also be present without symptoms; hydrops and Meniere's disease are not the same concept.
The first test is done two days after the last attack; otoscopy is normal in both ears.
The right ear has a loss of forty-five decibels at two hundred fifty and five hundred hertz, and thirty-five decibels at one thousand hertz.
Right bone conduction, measured with the left ear masked, overlaps air conduction; the loss is sensorineural.
From two thousand hertz up, right thresholds are near normal; so we see a loss that rises toward the high frequencies.
The left ear is within normal limits at all frequencies; left bone conduction is also around ten decibels.
Tympanograms are type A in both ears; so there is no middle ear problem that explains this loss.
Word recognition in the right ear is eighty-eight percent; because the loss is in the low frequencies, the score is relatively well kept.
The Barany Society criteria look for an audiometrically documented loss at two adjacent frequencies below two thousand hertz.
In this loss, the bone conduction threshold of the affected ear must be at least thirty decibels worse than the other ear's.
In our case, at two hundred fifty and five hundred hertz, right bone conduction is forty and left is ten decibels; a difference of thirty.
So the audiometric criterion is met; for this comparison, bone conduction must be correctly masked.
Definite Meniere's disease also requires at least two spontaneous vertigo attacks lasting twenty minutes to twelve hours.
Weighing the criteria as a whole and making the diagnosis is the physician's job; the audiologist provides the audiometric evidence.
One of the most distinctive features of Meniere's disease is that hearing fluctuates over time.
The red line shows the first measurement, two days after the last attack.
The green line is a follow-up test three weeks later, in a period without attacks; low-frequency thresholds improved by twenty decibels.
The purple line is a test two months later, right after a new attack; the low-frequency loss has returned, and is deeper.
The gray dashed line shows the healthy left ear; there is no change in that ear.
A single audiogram cannot show this fluctuation; this is why serial audiograms are so valuable.
The timing of each measurement relative to an attack is also recorded, because thresholds change with closeness to an attack.
To make serial measurements comparable, the same audiometer and the same type of earphones are used when possible.
The threshold method and masking rules are kept the same for every measurement.
At each test, the time of the last attack and that day's fullness and tinnitus are briefly noted.
Bone conduction is measured with masking every time; it is needed to document that the change is sensorineural.
In the report, results are shown side by side with earlier measurements; the physician sees the course at a glance.

maddeler.metin: _10 dB or more_ at adjacent frequencies
Bone conduction in the same direction?

cumleler: Repeated measurements in the same person usually differ by five decibels or less; such small differences do not count as fluctuation.
Repeated changes of ten decibels or more, in the same direction at adjacent frequencies, point more strongly to true fluctuation.
Bone conduction changing in the same direction as air conduction confirms that the change is sensorineural.
Comparing the word recognition score with the previous measurement also helps in understanding the course.
A test done close to an attack is expected to be worse; so no comparison is made without timing information.

notlar.metin: A normal ratio does not exclude hydrops

cumleler.yazi: For more information, the physician has requested electrocochleography, or ECochG.
cumleler.ses: For more information, the physician has requested electrocochleography, or E cock G.

cumleler.yazi: The summating potential, or SP, grows in hydrops; the action potential, or AP, does not grow to the same degree.
cumleler.ses: The summating potential, or SP, grows in hydrops; the action potential, or A P, does not grow to the same degree.

cumleler.yazi: In this example, the SP/AP ratio is zero point six zero in the right ear and zero point three zero in the left.
cumleler.ses: In this example, the S P over A P ratio is zero point six zero in the right ear and zero point three zero in the left.

cumleler: In the example, the lab's upper normal limit is zero point five zero; so the ratio in the right ear is considered elevated.
An elevated ratio, together with the history and the audiogram, supports the idea of endolymphatic hydrops.
But a normal ratio does not exclude hydrops; many people with Meniere's disease have a normal ratio.
Vestibular tests can also show a pattern typical of this disease.
The caloric test shows a forty percent unilateral weakness on the right; over twenty to twenty-five percent is usually significant.
In contrast, on the video head impulse test, or vHIT, gain in both lateral canals is normal and there are no corrective saccades.
This dissociation, a reduced caloric response with a normal vHIT, is often reported in Meniere's disease; hydrops is a proposed explanation.
Vestibular evoked myogenic potential, or VEMP, responses can also be affected; but findings vary from person to person.
None of these tests makes the diagnosis on its own; the diagnosis rests on clinical criteria.
Vestibular migraine can also bring attacks and ear symptoms; but a clear and lasting hearing loss is not expected.
This is why a history of migraine, headache and light sensitivity is asked about separately.
Unilateral sensorineural loss with vertigo may require the physician to investigate retrocochlear causes as well.
A low-frequency loss that comes as a single episode without vertigo is considered a different picture.
The picture should not be better explained by another vestibular diagnosis; the physician makes this distinction.
The audiologist's contribution here is to record the history in full and to present the audiometric finding clearly.
The audiologist's first task is to document the loss correctly, with masked thresholds and serial measurements.

cumleler.yazi: Tests the physician requests, such as ECochG, VEMP, caloric testing and vHIT, are done with standard protocols.
cumleler.ses: Tests the physician requests, such as E cock G, VEMP, caloric testing and vHIT, are done with standard protocols.

cumleler: In the report, measurements are given side by side and the timing of each measurement relative to an attack is written down.
Diagnosis and treatment are the physician's decisions; the audiologist suggests no drugs, diets or procedures, but stays in touch with ENT.
The audiologist also counsels the person about tinnitus and hearing and, when needed, discusses hearing support options.
If a new loss that seems lasting, or an attack of a different kind, occurs, the person is advised to see the physician without delay.

sahneler.metin: In a fluctuating loss, do not rely on a single measurement; note the timing relative to the attack at every test and keep conditions the same.
cumleler: A clinical tip: in a fluctuating loss, do not make decisions by looking at a single audiogram.
At every test, record when the last attack happened and how full the ear feels that day.
Use the same earphones and the same method as in the previous measurement; otherwise the source of a difference becomes unclear.
Do not skip two hundred fifty hertz, so that you do not miss small changes in the low frequencies.
The person is advised to sit or lie down somewhere safe as soon as an attack starts, because of the risk of falling.
A diary of the date and duration of attacks and the ear symptoms that come with them helps the physician's assessment a great deal.
Uncertainty and attacks can cause anxiety; it is important to explain that counseling and support exist for tinnitus and anxiety.
Not knowing when attacks will come makes daily life hard; even taking this complaint seriously brings relief.
If the loss becomes permanent, a hearing aid may be considered; with fluctuating thresholds, settings may need regular review.
Pure-tone: mild to moderate sensorineural hearing loss in the right ear, more marked in the low frequencies.
Course: about twenty-five to thirty decibels worse than before at two hundred fifty and five hundred hertz; tested right after an attack.

cumleler.yazi: ECochG: SP/AP ratio in the right ear above the lab limit.
cumleler.ses: E cock G: S P over A P ratio in the right ear above the lab limit.

cumleler: Vestibular tests: caloric weakness on the right, vHIT gains normal on both sides.
Advice: forward to the ENT physician with the findings; serial audiometry at intervals the physician advises.

maddeler.metin: SP/AP rise, caloric and vHIT dissociation

cumleler: In Meniere's disease, the loss often begins in the low frequencies and fluctuates with attacks.
Serial audiograms are taken under the same conditions and document the fluctuation; a single measurement cannot show it.

cumleler.yazi: An elevated SP/AP ratio and a caloric weakness with normal vHIT can support the picture, but do not make the diagnosis alone.
cumleler.ses: An elevated S P over A P ratio and a caloric weakness with normal vHIT can support the picture, but do not make the diagnosis alone.

cumleler: The physician makes the diagnosis using the Barany criteria; the audiologist provides measurements, reports and counseling.

sahneler.soru: The audiometric condition in the Barany criteria?
secenekler: 30 dB at two adjacent low frequencies
sahneler.aciklama: Bone conduction is at least 30 dB worse than the other ear at _two adjacent frequencies_ below 2000 Hz.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: in the Barany criteria, what is the audiometric condition for definite Meniere's disease?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: at least thirty decibels worse than the other ear, at two adjacent frequencies below two thousand hertz.
The comparison is made with bone conduction thresholds; so correct masking of bone conduction is essential.
